opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think world models are one of the most exciting directions right now, and honestly a bit underrated compared to all the attention on pure language models.

The way I think about it, there are a few big application areas. The first, and the one closest to my heart these days, is robotics. One of the hardest problems in robotics is data. With language we had the whole internet, but there's no internet-scale dataset of robots folding laundry or opening doors. A good world model, something that can predict how the physical world evolves when you take an action, lets you generate that experience in simulation. You can train a policy inside the world model, try thousands of variations, and fail cheaply before you ever touch real hardware. If that works well enough, it could unlock the same kind of scaling for robotics that we saw for text.

The second area is anything interactive: games, simulation, creative tools. Today we generate a video, and it's a fixed clip. With a world model you generate an environment you can step into and act in, and it responds to you. That's a different kind of medium. I think we'll see people building small interactive worlds the way they write a prompt today, and that's going to be a big creative playground.

The third one is more scientific, and a bit more speculative. Science is basically about building models of the world that let you predict "if I do this, what happens?" Today that's done with hand-written simulators in physics, chemistry, or biology. Learned world models could complement those, especially in messy domains where we don't have clean equations, like cell biology or weather at certain scales.

There's also a quieter point about AI agents generally. A lot of what we call reasoning is really planning: imagining consequences before acting. Language models do some of that in text, but grounding it in a model of how the world actually behaves, physically and causally, is probably part of getting agents that are reliable in the real world, not just on a screen.

What I'd really like to see, coming from the Hugging Face side, is for this to happen in the open. Right now a lot of the best world models sit inside a few labs. The datasets, the evaluation methods, even the definition of a "good" world model are still very immature. If we can get open models, open datasets of real-world interaction, and good open benchmarks, the robotics and research communities can iterate much faster. That's where I think the biggest potential is: making this a technology everyone can build on, not just a demo.

r001.rationale: It describes interactive, responsive worlds as a different kind of medium and a new creative playground, supporting a new form of virtual entertainment.

r002.rationale: It says world models can generate simulated robot experience for training policies before using real hardware.

r003.rationale: It discusses scaling robotics training through simulation, but does not suggest this would be the first breakthrough in simulated data generation in quite some time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think world models are where some of the most interesting stuff is going to happen over the next few years, honestly. Let me try to explain why I'm excited.

So right now, most of what we have in AI are models that are really good at a kind of static pattern matching. You give them text, they predict the next token. You give them an image, they tell you what's in it. And that's incredibly powerful, we've seen that. But it's fundamentally not how a human understands the world. When you reach for a cup, you're not predicting the next word, you're running a little simulation in your head: if I move my hand here, the cup will be there, the liquid will slosh this way. That's a world model. It's a predictive model of how the environment evolves when you act on it.

The potential, I think, is in three big areas. The first is robotics, which is the obvious one. Robots have been held back for decades because collecting data in the physical world is slow and expensive and you can break things. If you have a good world model, you can train in simulation, you can have the robot imagine the consequences of an action before it takes it. That changes the economics completely. At Hugging Face we've been pushing hard on open robotics with LeRobot precisely because we think this is coming, and we want the data and the models to be open rather than locked up.

The second is science and engineering. A world model that actually understands physics, or chemistry, or how a protein folds, is a very different thing from a language model that has read a lot of papers about physics. You can ask it counterfactual questions: what happens if I change this parameter? And it can answer by simulating rather than by retrieving. That's closer to how a scientist works.

And the third, which people underestimate, is just planning and agency in general. Even for digital agents, if a model can predict what a web page will look like after it clicks a button, or what the state of a codebase will be after it makes a change, it can plan several steps ahead instead of reacting blindly. A lot of what we call "agentic" behavior today is really trial and error. World models could make it deliberate.

Now, the caveat I'd add is that we're early. The video generation models are impressive, but a pretty video is not the same as a consistent physical model. Objects still disappear, gravity still gets a bit creative sometimes. The hard part is getting models that are consistent over long horizons and that respect the actual constraints of the world, not just the visual appearance of it. And I think the community needs open benchmarks and open models here, otherwise we'll end up with a handful of labs having world models and everyone else just getting an API. That's the part I personally care about a lot.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robotics, science and engineering, and digital-agent planning, but does not mention virtual entertainment.

r002.rationale: It says robots could be trained in simulation and imagine action consequences, but does not clearly identify generating simulated data for robots as an application.

r003.rationale: The response calls world models an emerging area, but does not suggest they would be the first breakthrough in simulated data generation in quite some time.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting potential is to move from systems that recognize patterns to systems that can predict what happens when you act. If a robot moves an object, how will that object behave? If it takes a particular path, what might it encounter? A world model could let it explore those possibilities before doing anything in the real world.

That could be very useful for robotics, where collecting experience is expensive and mistakes can break things. You could learn in simulation, try different strategies, and then transfer what you’ve learned. You can also imagine applications in games or in helping people design and test physical systems.

The big question is whether the model captures the things that matter for those decisions. Generating a plausible video is one thing; reliably predicting the consequences of an action is a much stronger requirement. That’s where I think a lot of the interesting work is.

r001.rationale: It mentions possible applications in games, but does not suggest an entirely new form of virtual entertainment.

r002.rationale: It describes learning and testing strategies in simulation for robotics, but does not identify generating simulated data for robots as an application.

r003.rationale: It discusses the promise and challenges of world models, but does not suggest they may be the first breakthrough in simulated data generation in quite some time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is moving from models that recognize patterns to models that can anticipate what happens when you take an action. If I move this object, what changes? If a robot takes this path, what will it encounter? A world model could let a system explore those possibilities before acting in the real world.

Robotics is an obvious application, because collecting real-world experience is slow and expensive. But you can also imagine applications in scientific discovery, where you simulate a process, propose an experiment, and then use the result to improve the model.

The difficult part is making those predictions reliable. A model can generate a very convincing video without understanding the underlying physics well enough to plan an action. So I’m excited about the potential, but the important test is whether these models actually help us make better decisions when we interact with the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses exploring possible actions before acting, but does not mention virtual entertainment or a new form of it.

r002.rationale: It names robotics as an application and says real-world experience is costly, but does not identify generating simulated data for robots.

r003.rationale: The response discusses the potential and reliability challenges of world models, but does not characterize simulated data generation as a breakthrough or say it has been a long time since one.
